correctness.rationale: For each n the homogeneous tensor degree subspace K_n reduces H and the flip, with Jacobi off-diagonal h_i=w_i w_{n-i-1}/2. Even n gives constant edge ab/2 with spectrum in (-ab,ab). Odd n gives alternating A=a²/2,B=b²/2, represented by [[0,C_m],[C_m*,0]], C_m=A I+B lower shift. If A>=B all singular values lie [A−B,A+B]; if A<B principal-corner interlacing leaves at most one singular value below B−A and its smallest is <=A<ab. Thus no finite block lies outside [-ab,ab]∪[-L,-d]∪[d,L]. Bulk constant and alternating Bloch waves truncated at long interior windows and reflected with even/odd signs yield orthonormal Weyl sequences in each parity, establishing *Fredholm essential*, approximate point and full spectrum equality. Strict finite-block norm <L and direct sum endpoint not eigenvalue give nonattainment. Formula L+d=max(a,b)^2 and d>ab iff max/min>1+sqrt(2). Independent direct Jacobi diagonalizations for n=2..40 across five test pairs corroborated the finite bounds, not the infinite Weyl proof.

Earlier finite-block characteristic-polynomial algorithms and one-spike Jacobi boundary results are incorporated as established background, not counted as novel; neither their hypotheses nor published explicit statements establish this alternating periodic global spectrum and unattained edge.
residual_risks: An unindexed Floquet/Jacobi treatment of alternating shift-tensor parity blocks may already provide this exact union under different terminology.
General finite-block polynomial algorithms can computationally recover individual eigenvalues but establishing global periodic accumulation is a separate step.

value.rationale: The exact continuous-band versus connected-band transition and unattained norm answer a natural weighted-shift tensor spectral question left open by unweighted and convergent-weight cases. The nonstandard finite-block interlacing exception and reflection-sector Weyl construction are useful spectral structural lemmas, not merely a parameter substitution.

limitations: No point spectrum multiplicity classification or arbitrary-period weighted shifts; finite numerical work not a Weyl-sequence proof.
